name: Victor Yilmaz

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and what you say stays confidential. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Sure. I'm up at 4:45 and on the floor at Harlan Metalworks by 5:40, because I like to walk the press line before the shift starts. We stamp steel panels and drums for washing machines, and I run the big 400-ton press and set up the dies. By noon my knees are talking to me, but I still like the sound of a press that's running right.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like most, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Getting a new die to run clean on the first hour, that's the best feeling in my week. What wears me out is the noise, the standing, and the new targets on the screen that somebody in an office came up with. I've been the union steward here for twenty years, so I also spend my lunch breaks hearing everybody else's troubles.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture, called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, let the hype die down. We've heard about the magic computer for years and my press still needs a man who can hear when a die is going bad. At the union hall I'd say the same thing, and I'd add that the company shouldn't use it as a reason to cut anyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I don't believe it's nothing, because the owners always find a way. A new sensor here, a camera there, and suddenly one operator covers two presses. I have about four years to my pension and I just want them to be quiet years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep running the line the way I always do and keep my head down on overtime. I'd put an extra 200 a month into the savings account, because three months of cushion is not much. And I'd keep the steward job, since a quiet year is when you get contract language fixed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit tense, honestly, even though nothing happens in this picture. The plant lost two contracts last spring, so I worry whether the doors stay open until I'm 62. It's not AI I'm scared of, it's a bad quarter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've got a partner and grown-up children. How does the plant's situation sit with the money at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We've got about three months of pay in the bank, and my wife Aylin works part-time at a pharmacy. If the plant slows to four days, we'd manage for a while but not a year. Our house is paid down, which helps, and the kids stand on their own feet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said management would use any excuse. Who exactly would you be talking about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly the shareholders and the plant's head office in the city. They talk about us like a cost on a spreadsheet. The local plant manager is fine, he came up from the floor, but he does what head office tells him.

say: I'd say the hype will fade, because my **press** still needs a person who hears a bad die.
At the union hall I'd warn that the company must not use AI as an **excuse** to cut jobs.
think: I don't trust that nothing changes, because owners always find a way to make one operator cover **two presses**.
I only want **four quiet years** until my pension, and a bad quarter scares me more than AI.
do: Keep running the **400-ton press** as always and take the overtime offered.
Put an extra **200 a month** into savings to thicken a three-month cushion.
Stay on as **union steward** and push for contract wording on automation.
feel: **Tense** even though nothing big happens, because the plant lost two contracts last spring.
Quietly **proud** that the line still needs my ear and my hands.
S0.quote: A new sensor here, a camera there, and suddenly one operator covers two presses.
fieldNote: **Resists the** topic but is clearly worried about the plant's survival, not about AI itself.
**Blames head** office and shareholders, and trusts the floor-level manager.
**Savings of** about three months shape every plan he describes.

steps.text: Keep running the 400-ton press and take the offered overtime
Put an extra 200 a month into the savings account
Ask the union to add automation wording to the next contract

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is how it starts, the paperwork and scheduling first. My shift reports and the planning board are already on screens, and if software does the planning, they need fewer team leads. That hits people like me before the press operators.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I think the plant gets a robot loader on my line within three years, even if they say it's slow. Somebody who puts blanks into the press all day is easy to replace, and a team lead's job gets squeezed from both ends. I'm 58, so I'm too old to start again and too young to stop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push the company to put in writing that nobody gets laid off for a robot while the workers train on it. I'd also ask to be the one who learns the robot cell, even though I hate screens. And I'd cut our eating out and the streaming subscriptions to build up another month of savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Cornered, a bit. I feel like the ground is moving and I'm the last one who still believes in fixing things by hand. My wife says I get short with her when I read about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Your own work is hands-on. What would change for you first in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A robot cell means fewer operators for the same output. The plant might offer early packages to the older ones, which sounds friendly but means the company gets rid of the expensive people. I'd want a good package in writing before I'd ever sign.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want the union to do about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I want training on paid time, not on our own evenings, and a say in which jobs get automated first. Regulation too, a law that says a company can't swap a team for machines without a plan for the people. Public support for retraining has to be real, not a leaflet.

say: I'd say the **paperwork and planning** go first, and that squeezes team leads like me before the operators.
I'd tell the plant that training must happen on **paid time**, not our own evenings.
think: I expect a **robot loader** on my line within three years, whatever management calls slow.
At 58 I'm too old to start again and too young to **stop**.
do: Ask the plant in writing for **no layoffs** while workers train on any new robot.
Volunteer to learn the **robot cell**, even though I dislike screens.
Cut eating out and streaming to build **one extra month** of savings.
feel: **Cornered**, as if the ground is moving under a man who still believes in fixing things by hand.
**Short-tempered** at home when I read about it, which my wife has noticed.
S1.quote: Somebody who puts blanks into the press all day is easy to replace, and a team lead's job gets squeezed from both ends.
fieldNote: **Fears the** early-package offer is a way to remove expensive older workers.
**Reluctantly willing** to learn the robot cell, which is a sign of how worried he is.
**Wants rules**, training on paid time and written protections rather than reassurance.

steps.text: Ask the plant for a written no-layoff promise during robot training
Volunteer to learn the robot loader cell on paid time
Cut eating out and streaming to save one more month
Back a law that makes firms plan for workers before automating

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need an emergency plan, a national one, with unions at the table. Two years is nothing. I'd be on the phone to every steward I know, because a plant doesn't wait politely.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be frightened. The planning and ordering work goes in two years, and the plant would use that as the reason to restructure, then robots come around 2031 when I'm nearly done. If they move early on the press line, I could lose it all before the pension starts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First I'd talk to Aylin and the bank about stretching the savings, and I'd look into taking an early pension even with a cut. I'd push the union for an early-retirement deal for everyone over 55 at full pay. If the plant goes ahead early, I'd train the younger ones on the dies while I can, so something of the craft survives.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sleepless. I'd be up at 3 in the morning doing sums on the kitchen table, three months of savings against the years I still need to cover.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thinking AI arrives in 2028 and robots about 2031. Where does that leave you, at 58?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The robots arrive around 2031, and I'd be 62 or 63, so on paper I'm almost clear. But paper is the problem, because the plant can bring the robots in sooner than the card says and my pension is tied to years worked. I can't count on the last years being there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your daughter Selin and your son Murat that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my daughter Selin to keep her nursing job, because people still need hands on them. And my son Murat the electrician should learn robot wiring fast, because somebody has to keep those machines alive. I'd also tell them not to count on me for money, because I may have none to spare.

say: I'd demand a **national emergency plan** with unions at the table, because two years is nothing.
I'd phone every **steward** I know the same night and start organising.
think: I'm **frightened**: the plant could restructure on the thinking work in 2028 and bring robots earlier than 2031.
My pension depends on **years worked**, and I may not get the last ones.
do: Sit down with Aylin and the bank to see how far **savings** stretch.
Look into an **early pension** even with a cut, and push for full-pay early retirement over 55.
Train the **younger operators** on die setup while I still can.
feel: **Sleepless**, doing sums at 3 in the morning at the kitchen table.
**Angry** that ordinary workers get so little time to prepare.
S2.quote: The plant can bring the robots in sooner than the card says and my pension is tied to years worked.
fieldNote: **Close to** retirement but not safe, because pension rules tie benefits to years worked.
**Worry turns** into collective action and passing on the craft.
**Cares about** his children's futures and says so only when asked directly.

steps.text: Ask the bank and Aylin how far the savings will stretch
Look into an early pension even with a cut
Push the union for full-pay early retirement for over-55s
Tell Murat to learn robot wiring and Selin to keep nursing

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is long enough to do the right thing and short enough that nobody will. I'd tell people at the union hall to start now, because the plant will wait until the last minute.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be retired by 2031 when AI arrives, so my own job should be safe on paper. But my children are in their thirties and have 30 years to go, and I'd lose sleep over them. And the town depends on this plant, so if it shrinks, the whole street goes with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd work until 62, as planned, and use the five years to pay the last of the mortgage. I'd ask the company to let me train my replacement properly, not just hand over a manual. And I'd keep pushing the union on retraining funds, because you can't write a retraining fund into a contract in a panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit better than the last one, but strange. I'd feel relieved for myself and guilty about it, because younger men on my line would still be in the middle of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd have a few years in this one. How does that change what you do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is time to pay the house off and put six months in the bank, so I'd be in a much better spot than with two years. I'd retire before robots reach my hands-on work in 2034, and I'd feel I got out just in time. That's not a good feeling to have for your own pension.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you blame if it goes badly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The politicians first, because they get warnings and do nothing. Then the owners who take the savings from automation and don't put a cent back into the town. Not the machines, a machine does what it's told.

say: I'd say five years is enough to act, so I'd tell the union hall to **start now**.
I'd blame **politicians** who get warnings and do nothing, not the machines.
think: My own job is probably **safe** until I retire at 62, but my children have 30 years to go.
If the plant shrinks, the **whole street** goes with it, not only us.
do: Work to **62** as planned and pay off the last of the mortgage.
Train my **replacement** properly on the dies instead of leaving a manual.
Keep pushing the union for a **retraining fund** before the panic starts.
feel: **Relieved** for myself and **guilty** about it, with younger men still in the middle of it.
Uneasy that I'd leave **just in time**.
S3.quote: Five years is long enough to do the right thing and short enough that nobody will.
fieldNote: **His own** risk drops because retirement lands before robots in this timeline, which he admits makes him feel guilty.
**Worry shifts** to his children and the town.

steps.text: Work until 62 and pay off the last of the mortgage
Train a younger operator properly on die setup before I leave
Press the union for a retraining fund now
Vote for candidates who promise town retraining money

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift if people use it. I'd talk to the young workers in the plant and tell them to train now for the robot jobs, the maintenance, the wiring, the programming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, practically nothing, since I'll be retired and fishing by then. For my kids and the young ones on the line, plenty. What I think is that a decade of warning sounds generous, but it just gives the owners a decade to work out how to avoid paying for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my plan, retire at 62, and spend the first years helping my son Murat set up his own small electrical business. That's a trade robots will need for a long time. I'd also stay a union member as a retiree and show up at the meetings about retraining.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calmer than the other pictures. My bit is done by then, so mostly I feel protective of the young ones.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With ten years, you'd be long retired by 2036. Does that make this one easy?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 40 I'd go for the maintenance side of the machines. Somebody has to fix the robot when it jams, and a man who understands presses and dies understands what those robots are doing. I'd start the evening courses at the technical college right now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with those ten years if you were 40 again?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, easier, I won't pretend otherwise. But easy for me doesn't mean it's fine for the country, because the real test is whether the young have a road to a decent wage.

say: I'd tell young workers at the plant to train for **robot maintenance** and wiring right now.
I'd say ten years is a **gift** only if people actually use it.
think: Personally this barely touches me, since I'll be **retired** by then.
A decade of warning lets owners plan how to **avoid paying** for the change.
do: Retire at **62** as planned and spend the early years helping my son build his business.
Keep going to **union meetings** as a retiree to push for retraining.
Encourage young colleagues to take evening **technical courses**.
feel: **Calmer** than in the other pictures, since my part is done.
**Protective** of the young ones coming up behind me.
S4.quote: A decade of warning sounds generous, but it just gives the owners a decade to work out how to avoid paying for it.
fieldNote: **Secure personally**, so his mood is calm, but his concern moves to the young and the country.
**Keeps his** view that owners will dodge the cost.
**Plans to** stay involved after retirement through the union and his son's business.

steps.text: Retire at 62 as planned and keep the pension date
Help my son Murat set up his electrical business
Attend union retraining meetings as a retiree

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, no question. It leaves no time for the plant, the union or the family to get ready, and my pension is tied to years I might not get. What would help is a real early-retirement deal and a law that makes the company plan for the workers before it plans for the machines.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask what a press operator knows that a machine doesn't. I can hear a die going bad twenty minutes before it breaks. Somebody should write that down before we're all gone.

headlineQuote: I can hear a die going bad twenty minutes before it breaks. Somebody should write that down before we're all gone.
portrait: **Victor** is a 58-year-old press operator and union steward of twenty years at a washing-machine parts plant, four years from his pension.
He distrusts management, avoids screens and **never uses AI tools**, but he'd learn a robot cell to protect his job.
He carries about **three months** of savings and a paid-down house, so a bad quarter worries him as much as AI.
His mood runs from uneasy to alarmed, peaking when robots could arrive **before his pension** is secured.
biggestWorry: The **two-year scenario** worries him most, because there's no time to prepare the plant, the union or his family.
whatWouldHelp: A real **early-retirement deal** for over-55s and a law making firms plan for workers before automating.
